title: Geometric fibres of a binomial plane curve
statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $a\in F$ and $C_a=\operatorname{Spec}F[x,y]/(xy-a)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-polynomial-ring]. This is a nonempty connected reduced scheme of pure dimension one [def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-pure-dimension]. If $a\ne0$, the map $x\mapsto z$, $y\mapsto az^{-1}$ identifies its coordinate ring with $F[z,z^{-1}]$, and $C_a$ is smooth over $F$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. If $a=0$, restriction to the two axes identifies its coordinate ring with
$$\{(f,g)\in F[x]\times F[y]:f(0)=g(0)\}.$$
Its irreducible components are the two affine lines $V(x)$ and $V(y)$; they meet scheme-theoretically in the single reduced point $(x,y)$. Its complement is smooth over $F$ and is the disjoint union of the two punctured axes. Each local ring has dimension at most one, and the local ring at $(x,y)$ has dimension one; explicitly its primes include the strict chain $(x)\subsetneq(x,y)$. All these conclusions persist after any extension of $F$. In particular, after extension to an algebraically closed field, the only nonsmooth point when $a=0$ is the crossing. Here reduced means having no nonzero nilpotents and local dimension means Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring].

proof.text: Put $A=F[x,y]/(xy-a)$ and denote the classes of the variables again by $x,y$. Suppose $a\ne0$. Then $x^{-1}=a^{-1}y$. The homomorphism $A\to F[z,z^{-1}]$ given by $x\mapsto z$, $y\mapsto az^{-1}$ is well defined since $z(az^{-1})=a$. Its inverse sends $z$ to $x$ and $z^{-1}$ to $a^{-1}y$: the latter elements multiply to $1$. The composites fix both generators on each side and hence every polynomial or Laurent polynomial. This proves the asserted $F$-algebra isomorphism, with no irreducibility assertion about $xy-a$ needed.

source.place: Agent explicit inverse maps; supporting Tag 00T6 (definition-standard-smooth).

proof.text: Still with $a\ne0$, the Laurent ring is a domain, being a subring of $F(z)$. Its spectrum is integral by the spectrum-of-domain theorem, hence reduced, irreducible and connected (an irreducible nonempty space cannot be partitioned into two nonempty clopen subsets). To compute dimension, write the Laurent ring as $F[z]_z$: fractions are precisely $p/z^n$, with equality tested after multiplication by a power of $z$. The localization-prime theorem shows that contraction of a prime is prime and that extension recovers it; thus contraction sends a strict prime chain to a strict prime chain of $F[z]$. The polynomial-dimension theorem bounds its length by one. The chain $(0)\subsetneq(z-1)$ in the Laurent ring has length one: evaluation at $z=1$ has quotient $F$, and $z-1\ne0$, also over $\mathbf F_2$. Thus its dimension is one. Its unique irreducible component is the whole spectrum, so it has pure dimension one.

source.place: Agent Laurent calculation; polynomial dimension and localization of primes, as in the cited general nodes.

proof.text: Now let $a=0$. The map $F[x,y]\to F[x]\times F[y]$, $h\mapsto(h(x,0),h(0,y))$, has kernel $(xy)$: vanishing of both restrictions means every nonzero monomial has positive $x$- and $y$-exponents, so is divisible by $xy$. Its image consists exactly of pairs with equal constant term. Indeed a pair $(f,g)$ with common constant $c$ is the image of $f(x)+g(y)-c$. This gives the asserted isomorphism. Each polynomial ring is a domain (the leading coefficient of a product of nonzero polynomials is nonzero), so their product, and its subring $A$, have no nonzero nilpotents. Each localization of $A$ is reduced: if $(b/s)^n=0$, some inverted $t$ satisfies $tb^n=0$, whence $(tb)^n=0$, so $tb=0$ and $b/s=0$. The stalk-localization theorem therefore makes $\operatorname{Spec}A$ a reduced scheme.

source.place: Agent restriction map and mixed-monomial kernel calculation; no external nodal-family criterion is used.

proof.text: Every prime of $A$ contains $x$ or $y$, since $xy=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Spec}A=V(x)\cup V(y)$. The quotient maps identify these closed subschemes with $\operatorname{Spec}F[y]$ and $\operatorname{Spec}F[x]$, respectively. Each is integral by the spectrum-of-domain theorem, so irreducible. Neither contains the other: their generic primes are $(x)$ and $(y)$, and the other variable is nonzero in the corresponding polynomial quotient. Any irreducible subset of a union of two closed sets lies in one of them, by the definition of irreducibility. Thus these are exactly the irreducible components. Both have dimension one by the polynomial-dimension theorem and the prime-chain/topological-dimension dictionary, proving purity. They are connected and share $(x,y)$; any clopen partition restricts trivially to each irreducible axis, and the shared point forces the same part for both, so the whole spectrum is connected and nonempty.

source.place: Agent prime/axis computation; supporting polynomial-dimension and spectrum-of-domain facts are the cited nodes.

proof.text: The scheme-theoretic intersection of the axes is $\operatorname{Spec}F$. The closed subschemes are $V(x)=\operatorname{Spec}A/(x)$ and $V(y)=\operatorname{Spec}A/(y)$, mapping to $\operatorname{Spec}A$ by the quotient maps. By the affine fibre-product theorem their fibre product over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is $\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(A/(x)\otimes_AA/(y)\bigr)$ with the projections induced by $a\mapsto a\otimes1$, $b\mapsto1\otimes b$. Here $A/(x)\otimes_AA/(y)\cong A/(x,y)$ via $\bar a\otimes\bar b\mapsto\overline{ab}$ (inverse $\bar c\mapsto\bar c\otimes1$), and $A/(x,y)=F[x,y]/(x,y)=F$. So the intersection is $\operatorname{Spec}F$, mapping to the prime $(x,y)$. Its single point is reduced because $F$ is a field. The complement of this point is $D(x)\amalg D(y)$: a prime $\mathfrak p\ne(x,y)$ cannot contain both $x$ and $y$, since $(x,y)$ is maximal (its quotient is $F$), so $\mathfrak p$ lies in $D(x)$ or $D(y)$; and $D(x)\cap D(y)=D(xy)=\emptyset$ since $xy=0$. In $A_x$, $y=xy/x=0$, giving $A_x=F[x,x^{-1}]$ by mutually inverse substitutions; similarly $A_y=F[y,y^{-1}]$. The principal-localization theorem identifies these rings with the two stated punctured-axis open subschemes.

source.place: Agent quotient/intersection universal property and punctured-axis coordinate calculation.

proof.text: In the zero case every increasing chain of primes of $A$ lies over one axis: its smallest prime contains $x$ or $y$, and then so do all larger primes. Quotienting by that variable gives a strict chain in a one-variable polynomial ring. Conversely inverse image under the quotient map preserves prime ideals and strict inclusions; these assertions follow directly from the definition of prime and surjectivity of the quotient map. Thus every chain has length at most one. The strict chain $(x)\subsetneq(x,y)$ exists, because the corresponding quotient chain in $F[y]$ is $(0)\subsetneq(y)$. In either case $a=0$ or $a\ne0$, the stalk-localization theorem and the localization-dimension theorem now bound every local dimension by one, using the global chain bounds of step 2 (transported along the isomorphism of step 1) and of this step. At the crossing the displayed chain ends at $(x,y)$, so its local dimension is exactly one.

source.place: Agent prime-chain argument; local-dimension statement of localization at a prime from the cited node.

proof.text: If $a\ne0$, $F[x,y]/(xy-a)$ has a standard smooth presentation: with first variable $x$ and one equation $xy-a$, the one-by-one Jacobian determinant is $y$, a unit with inverse $a^{-1}x$. The standard-smooth theorem gives a smooth ring map $F\to A$, and the theorem comparing smooth ring maps with smooth morphisms of affine schemes makes $C_a\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ smooth in the sense of the smooth-morphism definition. In the zero case each punctured axis is smooth for the same reason, using $F[z,w]/(zw-1)$, identified with $F[z,z^{-1}]$ by $z\mapsto z$, $w\mapsto z^{-1}$ and its inverse. Its Jacobian determinant with respect to $w$ is the unit $z$. Smoothness local on the source then proves that the complement of the crossing is smooth.

For $a=0$, the crossing is not smooth, already over $F$. Set $B=F[u,v]/(u^2,v^2)$, $I=(uv)$, and $\overline B=B/I$. The four monomials $1,u,v,uv$ form an $F$-basis of $B$, so $I^2=0$, $uv\ne0$, and $I=F\,uv$. The map $A\to\overline B$, $x\mapsto u$, $y\mapsto v$, defines a map from the affine first-order thickening $T=\operatorname{Spec}\overline B\subset T'=\operatorname{Spec}B$ to $C_0$. Both spectra have one point, mapping to the crossing, since $u,v$ are nilpotent and their quotient is $F$. If an open neighbourhood $U$ of the crossing were smooth, this map would factor through $U$ and formal smoothness would lift it to $T'\to U$. Its composite to the affine $C_0$ would give lifts of $u,v$ in $B$ whose product is zero. All such lifts have the form $u+cuv$, $v+duv$ with $c,d\in F$, and their product is $uv\ne0$, a contradiction. Together with step 7 this gives exactly the asserted nonsmooth locus, without using perfection or a characteristic assumption.

source.place: Tag 02H0 (definition-formally-smooth), Tag 02H6 (lemma-smooth-formally-smooth); agent explicit square-zero lifting obstruction.

proof.text: Finally let $F\hookrightarrow E$ be any field extension. The base-changed affine scheme is $\operatorname{Spec}E[x,y]/(xy-a_E)$. Explicitly, $E\otimes_F A\to E[x,y]/(xy-a_E)$ sends $e\otimes h$ to $e h$; its inverse sends $e$ to $e\otimes1$ and the variables to $1\otimes x,1\otimes y$. The tensor relations and the defining equation show both maps are well defined and inverse. By the affine fibre-product theorem, $C_a\times_{\operatorname{Spec}F}\operatorname{Spec}E\cong\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_FE)$, which is the base change of the definition; with the displayed isomorphism it is $C_{a_E}$ over $E$. Field embeddings preserve whether $a$ is zero. Apply steps 1--8 over $E$: the displayed substitutions, the axis ideals, the crossing quotient, the prime chains, the unit Jacobian entries and the monomial lifting obstruction use no property beyond being a field. This proves every conclusion after extension, including when $E$ is algebraically closed.
